Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,

  1
 closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

  7
 As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

SUBJECT:  MID-YEAR  BUDGET  REPORT  AND  ADJUSTMENTS  FOR  FISCAL  YEAR
2025-26

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:
  a.  Receive  the Fiscal  Year 2025-26  Mid-Year  Budget  Report  and Adjustments;
  b.  Approve  of Fiscal  Year 2025-26  Mid-Year  Adjustments;  and
  c.  Adopt  a Resolution  of the City  Council  of the City  of South  Gate Approving  Fiscal  Year
  2025-26  Mid-Year  Budget  Amendments  and Adjustments.

EXECUTIVE  SUMMARY

This report  updates  the Mayor,  City  Council,  and comrniu'iity  on the City's  financial  performance
for the first  half  of Fiscal  Year  2025-26  (July  through  December  2025),  presents  recommended
mid-year  budget  adjustments,  and provides  context  for  the FY  2026-27  budget  development
process.

The  City  closed  FY  2024-25  with  an unassigned  General  Fund  balance  of $9.4 million.  That
reserve  is projected  to be nearly  fully  consumed  by the end of the current  fiscal  year, leaving  an
estimated  balance  of approximately  $1.O million.  This  drawdown  reflects  a structural  imbalance
between  ongoing  revenues  ($71.9  million  projected)  and ongoing  expenditures  ($82.5  million
projected),  resulting  in an operational  deficit  of approximately  $10.6 million.

Cost pressures  largely  outside  the City's  control  are the primary  driver.  Since FY 2019-20,  pension
obligations,  employee  health  insurance,  liability  and workers'  compensation  insurance,  and street
lighting  and landscaping  costs have increased  by a combined  $10.7 million  annually  -  an amount
that  exceeds  the  entire  structural  deficit.  At  the  same  time,  revenues  have  underperformed,
particularly  sales tax, which  has contracted  approximately  l 1.9%  over the past thirteen  quarters
due in part  to the permanent  closure  of a major  auto  dealership.  Federal  ARPA  fiinding  that
previously  helped  bridge  this gap has been fully  expended.

Through  December  2025,  the City  collected  $18.2  million  in General  Fund  revenues  (24.6%  of
budget)  and spent $33.0  million  (40.8%  of budget),  consistent  with  historical  mid-year  patterns.
No  new  General  Fund  appropriations  are requested.  Proposed  adjustments  are limited  to non-
General  Fund accounts,  grant-funded  programs,  and reallocation  of existing  authority.

  I
  9
 With  reserves  being  used to balance  the budget,  the FY 2026-27  budget  will  require  meaningfiil
decisions  about  service  levels  and expenditures.  All  departments  have  received  instructions  to
identify  reductions,  and a comprehensive  plan  will  be presented  to the City  Council  during  the
upcoming  budget  process.

Staff requests  that the City  Council  receive  and approve  this Mid-Year  Budget  Report  and adopt
the associated  resolution  approving  mid-year  budget  amendments.  The complete  report  follows.

BACKGROUND

On July 22, 2025,  the City  Council  adopted  the Fiscal  Year  (FY)  2025-26  0perating  and Capital
Improvement  Program  (CIP)  budgets.  The  FY  2025-26  Budget  serves  as the City's  financial
operating  plan, establishing  organizational  goals, budget  priorities,  and service  levels  for the fiscal
year, and identifying  the resources  necessary  to deliver  those services.

The adopted  budget  is based  on a series  of revenue  and expenditure  assumptions.  As the year
progresses,  changes  in  economic  conditions,  grant  awards,  and  operating  needs  necessitate
periodic  adjustments  to appropriation.  In many  cases, these  adjustments  allow  departments  to
spend newly  awarded  grant  funds  for which  no appropriation  currently  exists,  or to align  multi-
year grants  and capital  projects  with  final  award  amounts.  In other cases, adjustments  are required
to reflect  contractual  obligations  or operational  changes  that were not 'fully  known  at the time  of
budget  adoption.

The FY  2025-26  Mid-Year  Financial  Review  reports  on the City's  fiscal  performance  for  the
period  of July through  December  2025. The report  primarily  focuses  on the General  Fund,  which
supports  core  municipal  services,  including  law  enforcement,  public  works,  and  parks  and
recreation.

The  City  currently  faces  a structural  budget  deficit  in which  ongoing  operating  expenditures
exceed  ongoing  revenues.  Prior  fiscal  year budgets-maintained  service  levels  by using  one-time
resources,  including  federal  American  Rescue  Plan Act (ARPA)  funding,  interfund  transfers,  and
planned  use of fiind  balance.  Those  temporary  resources  are now  largely  exhausted  and are no
longer  available  to support  ongoing  operations.  As a result,  future  budgets  must increasingly  rely
on aligning  recurring  revenues  with  recurring  expenditures.  In the absence  of new  recurring
revenue  sources,  the City will  need to implement  expenditure  reductions  to bring  the General  Fund
into structural  balance.

ANALYSIS:

FY 2024-25  Year  End

At the end of each fiscal year, the Administrative  Services  Department  begins  its process  of closing
out the year.  This  process  includes  reconciling  the budget  and ensuring  all capital  improvement
project  carryovers  are processed  and reflected  in the new fiscal  year. In addition,  to avoid  potential
budget  inflation,  at the end of each fiscal  year,  all purchase  orders  and encumbrances  are closed
out, except  for multi-year  capital  projects.

FY 2025-26  Changes  from  Adopted  Budget  to Mid-Year  Budget

When  the FY  2025-26  budget  was presented  to City  Council  for  consideration  in July  2025,
economists  were discussing  concerns  about  inflation,  a 3.2%  CPI increase,  and Federal  Reserve
interest  rate  adjustments  aimed  at curbing  it. The  City  of South  Gate  anticipated  a moderate
increase  in property  tax,  offset  by a reduction  in sales tax. As the fiscal  year has progressed,
revenues  have underperformed  adopted  budget  projections  in several  key categories,  most notably
Sales Tax, reflecting  both regional  economic  softness  and the permanent  loss of a major  point-of-
sale business.  These  developments  reinforce  the importance  of continued  monitoring  of monthly
receipts  and disciplined  expenditure  management  through  the close of the fiscal  year.

  *  General  Sales Tax  and Measure  P General  Purpose  1% Local  Sales Tax  are performing
  lower  than anticipated.

  *  The American  Rescue  Plan Act of 2021 created  the State and Local  Fiscal  Recovery  Fund
  (SLFRF).  The City  received  $34,556,473  in SLFRF  Funds  which  have been programmed
  in annual  city budgets  beginning  in FY 2021-22.

The FY 2025-26  budget  included  significant  impacts  due to anticipated  rising  costs in insurance
premiums,  annual  increases  to the City's  Unfunded  Accrued  Liability  (UAL)  pension  payments,
the  need  to  invest  in  aging  capital  infrastructure,  and  support  of  the  Street  Lighting  and
Landscaping  Fiu'id. The proposed  mid-year  review  and adjustments  include  as-needed  pool repairs
at swim  stadium  and fireworks  show in July 2026 marking  the 250'h birthday  of the United  States.
Several  revenue  categories  are projected  to increase  modestly,  including  Fines  and Forfeitures,

 FY 2025-26  Mid-Year  Revenue  Performance

Total  General  Fund revenue  as of mid-year  FY 2025-26  is $18,179,542,  which  is approximately
24.6%  of the Adopted  General  Fund  revenues  of $73.8  million,  including  Transfers  In. Outlined
below  is a summary  of the revenue  performance  for the City's  major  revenues:

Property  Tax
Property  Tax is the City's  second-largest  General  Fund  revenue  source.  The FY 2025-26  budget
assumes property  tax revenues  of $18,601,976.  Through  December  2025, property  tax receipts  are
$1,398,465  higher  than  the same period  in FY 2024-25.  Property tax revenues  are received
primarily  in December  and April  following  the County's  property  tax distribution  schedule.  Based
on  current  information,  staff  does  not  recommend  adjusting  the  FY  2025-26  property  tax
projection  at this time.

Sales Taxes
Sales Tax revenues  totaled  $4,361,261,  or 29.3%  of the annual  budget.  Collections  are below  the
expected  mid-year  pace, reflecting  both regional  economic  headwinds  and local business-specific
factors  that have reduced  the City's  sales tax base during  the current  fiscal  year.

At the regional  level,  Los Angeles  County's  adjusted  sales tax growth  was essentially  flat in 3Q
2025 compared  to the prior  year, while  South Gate's adjusted  receipts  declined  5.0% over the same

  5

  13
 period.  This  underperformance  relative  to county  peers  is consistent  with  a broader  multi-year
trend:  on an inflation-  and economic-adjusted  basis,  South  Gate's  sales tax base has contracted
approximately  11.9%  over the past thirteen  quarters,  a pattern  that reflects  structural  changes  in
the City's  retail  and commercial  activity  rather than cyclical  economic  conditions  alone.

The Autos  and Transportation  sectors have experienced  the most significant  decline,  driven  by the
closure  of a major  auto  dealership  during  the current  fiscal  year.  This  represents  a permanent
reduction  in point-of-sale  revenue  rather  than  a temporary  fluctuation,  and the  sector  is not
expected  to recover  to prior-year  levels  in the near term.  HdL  projects  the category  to decline
approximately  18% for the full  fiscal  year before  stabilizing  modestly  in FY 2026-27.

The  General  Consumer  Goods  sector,  which  represents  the City's  largest  revenue  category  at
approximately  26% of total point-of-sale  receipts,  has shown  modest  softness  on an adjusted  basis,
consistent  with  broader  trends  in consumer  discretionary  spending  driven  by elevated  household
debt  levels  and reduced  discretionary  income.  The  Firestone  Boulevard  commercial  corridor,
which  generates  the majority  of the City's  point-of-sale  revenue,  experienced  an 11.3%  decline  in
3Q 2025  compared  to the prior  year,  underscoring  the City's  concentration  risk  within  a single
commercial  corridor.

Based  on HdL's  mid-year  analysis,  the FY 2025-26  Sales Tax revenue  estimate  has been revised
downward  by  $1,688,875  from  the  adopted  budget.  This  revised  projection  reflects both the
permanent  revenue  loss from  the dealership  closure  and continued  softness  in consumer-facing
categories.  HdL's  current  mid-year  estimate  is lower  than its prior  quarter  forecast,  indicating  that
the risk to revenue  remains  on the downside.  A slow recovery  is anticipated  beginning  in FY 2026-
27, with  modest  growth  projected  across most industry  segments  as economic  conditions  stabilize.

Other  Taxes
Other Taxes include  Transient  Occupancy  Tax, Business  License  Tax, Franchise  Tax, Commercial
Refuse  Franchise  Tax,  Real  Estate  Transfer  Tax,  and Materials  Recovery  Facility  Tax.  These
revenues  totaled  $1,150,054,  or 18.78% of the annual  budget.  Collections are slightly below pace,
primarily  due to the transition  of Business  License  Tax  administration  to HdL,  a consultant
specializing  in local  government  tax programs.  As HdL's  processes,  billing  cycles,  discovery,  and
enforcement  efforts  are fully  implemented,  Business  License  Tax  collections  are expected  to
strengthen  in subsequent  quarters.  Franchise  Tax revenues  are projected  to decrease  by $294,725
from  the adopted  budget  to $1.8 million.  In total,  the estimated  FY 2025-26 0ther Taxes revenue
is projected  to decrease  by $303,055  to $24.4 million.

Licenses  & Permits
Licenses  and Permits  revenue  totaled  $540,210  or 31.9%  of the annual  projection.  This  category
is generally  on pace,  supported  by steady  activity  in building  permits  and development-related
services.  A portion  of this category,  animal  licensing  revenue,  will  not be recorded  until  the close
of FY 2025-26,  temporarily  moderating  mid-year  results.  The estimated  revenue  for FY 2025-26
will  decrease  by $134,833  to $1.5 million.

Fines  & Forfeitures

includes  parking  citations,  code enforcement  fines,  and other  penalties.  Collections  are slightly
below  target  but  remain  generally  consistent  with  historical  mid-year  patterns.  The  estimated
revenue  for FY 2025-26  will  increase  by $115,412,  to $1.6 million.

Use of Money  & Property
Use of Money  & Property  generated  $1,330,972,  or 53.8%  of the annual  budget.  This  category
includes  interest  earnings  and lease revenues.  Interest  income  was substantial  through  mid-year
due to elevated  interest  rates. The Federal  Reserve  has recently  begun reducing  rates and may  do
so again, which  could moderate  investment  earnings  going  forward.  The estimated  revenue  for FY
2025-26  will  increase  by $131,036  to $2.6 million.

Intergovernmental
Intergovernmental  revenue  totaled  $179,216,  or 15.6%  of the  aru'iual  estimate.  This  category
includes  grants and Motor  Vehicle-In-Lieu  Excess  revenue.  Mid-year  receipts  appear lower  under
a straight-4ine  assumption  because  a $921,000  California  for All  Youth  Workforce  Program  Grant
is  reimbursable;  revenue  is  recognized  only  after  eligible  expenditures  are  incurred  and
reimbursed.  The estimated  revenue  for FY 2025-26  will  decrease  by $13,783  to $1.1 million.

Fees & Charges
Fees &  Charges  generated  $1,702,385,  or 42.5%  of the annual  budget,  making  it one of the
strongest  performing  categories.  This  revenue  includes  plan  check  fees,  passport  services,
recreation  program  revenues,  inspection  fees, and other user-based  charges.  Strong  participation
in  City  programs  and  steady  zoning,  plaru'iing,  and  inspection  activity  contributed  to  this
performance.  The estimated  revenue  for FY 2025-26  will  decrease  by $754,257  to $3.2 million.

Other  Revenues
Other  Revenues  totaled  $2,779,873, or 48.1%  of the annual  projection.  This  category  includes
Administrative  Allocations,  Miscellaneous  Reimbursements,  and  Miscellaneous  Revenue.
Administrative  Allocations  are recorded  in December  and the following  June, so revenues  in this
category  are expected  to increase  in the fourth  quarter.  The estimated  revenue  for FY 2025-26  will
increase  by $620,817 to $6.4 million.

Total  General  Fund  expenditures  for the mid-year  of FY 2025-26  were $32,982,202  or 40.8oA of

operational  activities,  staffing,  and project  schedules.

The  Administrative  Services  Department  will  continue  to  monitor  expenditures,  address

Table  4  presents  the  updated  FY  2025-26  Financial  Forecast,  incorporating  year-to-date
performance,  previously  approved  budget  actions,  and  the  mid-year  budget  adjustments
recommended  in this  report.  The third  column  reflects  the Revised  Budget,  which  includes  all
unanticipated  expenditures  and proposed  adjustments.  Based on this revised  forecast,  the projected
FY 2025-26  General  Fund  ending  fund balance  is $1,210,301.

The structural  imbalance  reflected  in this  forecast  is primarily  driven  by increases  in operating
costs that have grown  faster than available  revenue  sources,  many  of which  are outside  the City's
direct control. Since FY 2019-20, pension  obligations  have  increased  by  approximately  $4.3
million,  health  insurance  costs by approximately  $2.2 million,  workers'  compensation  and general
liability  insurance  premiums  by approximately  $3.3  million,  and street  lighting  and landscape
maintenance  costs by approximately  $0.9 million.  Together,  these four categories  alone represent
more  than  $10.7 million  in additional  annual  costs -  an amount  that exceeds  the City's  entire
projected  structural  deficit  and  reflects  expenses  that  are  largely  fixed  and  not  subject  to
discretionary  reduction.  Similar  cost pressures  are being  experienced  by cities  across California.

While  the FY 2025-26  deficit  can be addressed  through  the use of reserves,  the City  continues  to
face a structural  imbalance  between  recurring  revenues  and expenditures.  This  drawdown  will
reduce  the unassigned  General  Fund  balance  from  $9.4 million  at the close  of FY  2024-25  to
approximately  $1.2 million,  a near-depletion  of the City's  available  reserves  that leaves  limited
capacity  to  absorb  further  shocks  in  the  current  or future  fiscal  years.  The  City  Council's
consideration  of a fiscal  emergency  declaration  in January  2026  reflected  the severity  of this
structural  gap, estimated  at $8-9.4 million  in recurring  costs. The FY 2026-27  budget  development
process  will  focus  on  identi:[ying  long-term  solutions  to  restore  structural  balance.  Budget
instructions  have been issued  to all departments,  directing  them  to identi'Jy  reductions,  and the
proposed  expenditure  reduction  plan by department  will  be presented  to the City  Council  as part
of the FY 2026-27  budget  process.

FISCAL  IMP ACT:
The recommended  mid-year  budget  adjustments,  combined  withthe  updated  FY 2025-26  financial
forecast,  keep the General  Fund  aligned  with  projected  year-end  actual  results.  The overall  fiscal
impact  is a projected  decrease  to the General  Fund  balance  of $10,622,860  in FY  2025-26,  as
detailed  in Table  4. This  deficit  is funded  by a planned  drawdown  of Budget  Stabilization  and
unassigned  reserves,  reducing  the projected  unassigned  General  Fund  balance  from  $9.4 million
to approximately  $1.2 million.  This  use of reserves  represents  a one-time bridge while the City
develops  structural  budget  solutions  for :tuture fiscal  years.  Given  the limited  remaining  reserve
capacity,  there is no financial  cushion  to absorb  additional  unbudgeted  costs without  returning  to
Council  for further  action.  To place the structural  challenge  in context:  the City's  entire  General
Fund revenue  base is approximately  $71 million,  and a structural  gap of $8 to $9 millionrepresents
roughly  13 percent  of annual  General  Fund revenues.  Addressing  a deficit  of this magnitude  will
require  significant  policy  decisions  regarding  service  levels,  staffing,  and  operational
expenditures;  decisions  that cannot  be resolved  through  one-time  measures  alone.

During  the remainder  of the fiscal  year, if any material  variances  or additional  funding  needs arise,
staff will  rehirn  to the City  Council  with  recommended  budget  adjustments.

  CITY  OF SOUTH  GATE

  A RESOLUTION  OF THE  CITY  COUNCIL  OF THE  CITY  OF SOUTH  GATE
  APPROVING  FISCAL  YEAR  2025-2026  MID-YEAR  BUDGET  ADJUSTMENTS

  WHEREAS,  on July  22, 2025,  the City  Council  adopted  the Fiscal  Year  2025-2026
Budget;

  WHEREAS,  since the adoption  in July 2025,  City  Council  has taken  action  to adjust  the
general  ledger  of the Fiscal  Year 2025-2026  Budget  to fund various  projects  across the agency;

  WHEREAS,  at the March  10, 2026  City  Council  meeting,  the City  Council  considered
recommended  Mid-Year  Budget  Adjustments  to the Fiscal  Year 2025-2026  Budget;

  WHEREAS,  the City  Council  considered  amending  the Fiscal  Year  2025-2026  Budget
to include  Capital  Improvement  Program  (CIP)  appropriations,

  WHEREAS,  the City  Council  desires to amend  the Fiscal  Year 2025-2026  Budget;

NOW,  THEREFORE,  THE  CITY  COUNCIL  OF  THE  CITY  OF  SOUTH  GATE,
CALIFORNIA,  DOES  HEREBY  RESOLVE  AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION  1.  The Fiscal  Year  2025-2026  Budget  is hereby  amended  to reflect  those  Adjusted
Budget  amounts  for  Fund  Sources  and  Accounts  as stated  in the  FY  2025-2026  Mid-Year
Revenue  Adjustments  (Attachment  1) and FY  2025-2026  Mid-Year  Expenditure  Adjustments
(Attachment  2);

SECTION  2. All  other terms  of the Fiscal  Year 2025-2026  Budget,  and prior  adjustments  to the
general  ledger  of  the  Fiscal  Year  2025-2026  Budget,  not  amended  herein  shall  remain
unchanged;  and

SECTION  3.  The Fiscal  Year  2025-2026  Budget  is hereby  amended  to include  the budgeted

The Planning  Commission  approved  the development  of a general  quick-service  restaurant  (QSR)  with
a drive-through  and walk-up  window  onthree  lots. An existing  3,680-square-foot  (SF) vacant  restaurant

BACKGROUND:

Site History  and Environmental  Setting
The overall  site for development  of the drive-through  restaurant  involves  three lots: one developed  lot
and two lots used for parking.  The developed  lot (4816  Firestone  Boulevard)  at the northwestern  portion
of the site has a one-story,  3,680  SF commercial  building  built  in 1928,  which  has been used as a
restaurant.  The property  at 8915 Vossler  Avenue  has been used as a parking  lot for the restaurant  for
decades and is the subject  of this application.

The overall  site is bounded  by Firestone  Boulevard  to the north,  Vossler  Avenue  to the east, residential
uses to the south,  and commercial  uses to the west. The Azalea  Shopping  Center  is located  north  of the
site across Firestone  Boulevard.  The overall  site is flat with  paved  sidewalks  along the streets. An alley

 traverses  the site from  the east to the west. Vegetation  is minimal,  limited  to a few street trees along
Vossler  Avenue  and a planter  area at the northeastern  corner.  The southern  parking  lot has a planter
area along Vossler  Avenue,  which  has not been maintained.  There  are no sensitive  habitats  or protected
species  in the area. Wildlife  consists  of common  urban birds  and small mammals.  There  are no known
historical,  cultural,  or scenic  designations  on the property.

lot. The three lots are all rectangular-shaped  with  an alley traversing  the project  site. The subject  site at
8915 Vossler  measures  128.2 feet deep by 60 feet wide according  to the County  Assessor's  map. Table

Zone Change  (ZC No. 25-01 ) and General  Plan Amendment  (GPA  No. 25-01 )
The applicant  proposes  a Zone  Change  to change  the zone from  NL  to UN  and remove  the Corridor

Density  Residential  to Commercial  for the property  at 8915 Vossler  Avenue.  The 'UN zoning  district

January  20, 2026,  the Planning  Commission  recommended  to the City  Council  approval  of the Zone
Change  and General  Plan Amendment.  The Planning  Commission  included  a condition  of approval
requiring  the lot at 8915 Vossler  Avenue  to be linked  in perpetuity  to the northern  lots to prevent  it
from  being  sold separately,  potentially  eliminating  much  of the parking.

Vossler  Avenue  has historically  been  used  as a parking  lot  serving  adjacent  commercial  uses.  In
addition,  the proposed  {JN zoning  designation  permits  residential  development  at densities  of up to 40
dwelling  units  per acre,  compared  to the 9-16  dwelling  units  per acre allowed  under  the Medium
Density  Residential  land use designation.  Accordingly,  the Zone  Change  is consistent  with  the City's
Housing  Element  and would  not result  in a loss of housing  opportunity;  rather,  it would  facilitate  the
potential  for increased  residential  development.  The Zone  Change  and General  Plan Amendment  are

2.  EXEMPTION  RATIONALE

Article 19, Categorical  Exemptions,  or the State CEQA Guidelines  (Sections  15300-15333)  lists

classes  of projects  which  have  been  determined  not  to  have  a significant  effect  on the
environment  and which are exempt  from the provisions  of CEQA as required  by Section  2al084 of

the Public  Resources  Code.  This section  provides  an analysis  demonstrating  that the Project
meets the conditions  for a Class 3 Categorical  Exemption  and that none ofthe  possible  exceptions
to a Categorical  Exemption  listed in Section  15300.2  of the State CEQA  Guidelines  is applicable
to this Project.  The specific  language  of the Class 3 Categorical  Exemption  and each possible
exception  is shown  in italics  below  under  their respective  headings,  which  are followed  by the
Project analysis  for each condition  and exception.

3.  PROJECT  ANALYSIS  OF CONDITIONS  CONSISTENCY

  a)  Conditions  of the  Class  3 Categorical  Exemption

[State CEQA Guidelines Sectionl 15303. New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures

Class  3 consists  of construction  and location  of limited  numbers  of new,  small  facilities  or

structures;  installation  of small  new  equipment  and  facilities  in small  structures;  and  the

conversion  of existing  small structures  from one use to another  where  only minor modifications
are made in the exterior  of the structure.  The numbers  of structures  described  in this section  are

the maximum  allowable  on any legal parcel.  Examples  of this exemption  include,  but are not
limited  to:

(a) One single-family  residence,  or a second  dwelling  unit in a residential  zone.  In urbanized
areas,  up to  three  single-family  residences  may  be  constructed  or converted  under  this
exemption.

(b) A dupjex or similar  multi-family  residential  structure,  totaling  no more than four dwelling  units.

In urbanized  areas,  this  exemption  applies  to apartments,  duplexes  and  similar  structures
designed  for not more than six dwelling  units.

Discussion: As discussed in the Project Description above, the Project consists of the
construction of an approximately 1,700-square foot fast-food restaurant with drive-through and
walk-up service.

As quoted above, the CEQA Guidelines for a Class 3 Categorical Exemption includes the example
of a restaurant not exceeding 2,500 square feet of floor area, or 10,000 square feet of floor area
in urbanized areas. The Project would construct a restaurant smaller than both sizes referenced
in the Class 3 examples, within an urbanized area. Therefore, given the size of the proposed
restaurant, the Project fits within the definition of a small structure.

The Project Site is also within an urbanized area, and the Project would not require the use of
significant amounts of hazardous substances. The Project Site is within an area where all public
services and facilities are available.

With respect to environmentally sensitive areas, the Project Site is not within a designated or
proposed Significant Ecological Area.' Furthermore, the Project Site is located within an
urbanized and developed area, and the site is entirely developed and paved; the Project would
not disturb any previously undisturbed or natural areas.

These findings demonstrate that the Project consists of the construction and location of limited
numbers of new, small facilities or structures. The Project, therefore, meets the requirements of
a Class 3 Categorical Exemption pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15303.

  C. Vehicle  Miles  Traveled  (VMT) Analysis

  In response to Senate Bill (SB) 743, the California Natural Resource Agency certified and adopted new
  CEQA Guidelines in December 2018 which now identify Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) as the most
  appropriate metric to evaluate a project's transportation impact under CEQA (§ 15064.3).

  Effective July "1,2020, the previous CEQA metric of LOS, typically measured in terms of automobile
  delay, roadway capacity and congestion, generally will no longer constitute a significant environmental
  impact.

  Based on Section 3.1.2.1 of the County of Los Angeles traffic study requirements (July 23, 2020),
  retail projects with less than 50,000 square feet of area are screened out from requiring a full VMT
  analysis. A copy of the guidelines is contained in Attachment B.

  Hence, the proposed project is expected to screen out for requiring a full VMT analysis and the project
  is forecast to have a less than significant VMT impact.

  SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  TO APPROVE  THE  RECLASSIFICATION  OF THE  FULL-
  TIME  EXECUTIVE  ASSIST  ANT  POSITION  IN THE  PUBLIC  WORKS  DEPARTMENT
  TO  A  FULL-TIME  PUBLIC  WORKS  SPECIAL  PROJECTS  COORDINATOR
  POSITION

  PURPOSE:  To approve  the reclassification  of the full-time  Executive  Assistant  position  in the
  Public  Works  Department  to a full-time  Public  Works  Special  Projects  Coordinator  position.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The  City  Council  will  consider  adopting  a Resolution  to
  approve  the reclassification  of the 'full-time  Executive  Assistant  position  in the Public  Works
  Department  to a full-time  Public  Works  Special  Projects  Coordinator  position.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  The reclassification  of the full-time  Executive  ASSistant  position  to a Public
  Works  Special  Projects  Coordinator  position  in the Public  Works  Department  will  result  in an
  estimated  savings  of  approximately  $17,000  annually,  which  includes  the  cost  of  benefits.
  Additionally,  as a result  of this reclassification,  it will  result  in the elimination  of one (1) Office
  Assistant  position  for Fiscal  Year 2026/27  which  will  yield  an additional  savings  of approximately
  $78,000,  for a total  savings  of $95,000  in General  Funds.

  ANALYSIS:  None.

  BACKGROTJND:  The City must, from  time to time, add, remove,  reclassify,  or otherwise  adjust
 job  classifications,  job  specifications  and/or  compensation  in the Salary  Resolution  and Position
  Classification  Plan in order to satisfy  the changing  needs and demands  of the City's  workforce.  In
  response  to these changing  needs and demands,  job classification  specifications  must be amended
  to more  closely  match  the tasks wich  need to be performed  by employees  in the City's  various
  departments.

  As the demands  of the City  Council,  City  Manager,  and Department  Heads began to change  over
  the yearj;  so have  the duties  and requirements  of the administrative  positions  providing  direct
  support  to executive-level  management.  Traditionally,  these direct  support  staff positions,  such as
  a secretary  or executive  assistant,  would  aid the department  director  in the preparation  of dictated

  1

  112
 letters,  calendar  management,  preparation  of documents,  and other similar  administrative  support
functions.  However,  as technology  has improved  in the 21s' Century,  department  heads are able to
manage  their  calendars  and correspondence  through  their  desktop  computers,  manage  their  phone
calls, and perform  most of the functions  of a traditional  secretary  or executive  assistant.  Today's
department  head is in need of some administrative  support;  however,  what  is in more  demand  is
the department  head's  need to have  someone  capable  of performing  research,  preparing  agenda
bills,  and other lower-level  analytical  functions.  In some cases, this role may be filled  by an analyst
if the intended  duties  are complex,  while  in other  cases, this role may be filled  by an individual
capable  of performing  administrative  support  duties  as well  as some analytical  functions,  which
are called  Special  Project  Coordinators

The Public  Works  Department's  long serving  Executive  Assistant  retired  with  more than 30 years
of service  at the end of February  2026,  which  now permits  the City  to reevaluate  the needs of the
Public  Works  Department  and, as stated previously,  the duties  of what  this position  should  do in
support  of the Public  Works  Director  has dramatically  evolved  over the last three decades.  Further,
in an effort  to ensure the City  is "right  sizing"  its workforce,  the Public  Works  Department  needs
a Special  Projects  Coordinator  to replace  the position  of Executive  Assistant.

The  Public  Works  Special  Projects  Coordinator  will  perform  a hybrid  range  of  advanced
executive-level  administrative  support  and entry-level  analytical  duties  to support  the day-to-day
operational  and prograrnmatic  needs  of the  Department.  The  Public  Works  Special  Projects
Coordinator  will  also perform  highly  responsible  professional  administrative  work,  with  a primary
focus on coordinating  and tracking  assigned  special  projects,  while  also providing  executive-level
administrative  support.  This  position  will  be paid  consistent  with  the  City's  existing  Special
Projects  Coordinator  position  at Pay Grade  640.

Accordingly,  City  staff  recornrnends  approving  this  action  to reclassify  the Executive  Assistant
position  in the Public  Works  Department  to the Public  Works  Special  Projects  Coordinator.

 MEEDER  PUBLIC  FUNDS,  INC.  FOR  DISCRETIONARY  INVESTMENT
 MANAGEMENT  SERVICES

PURPOSE: To approve a Professional Services Agreement with Meeder Public Funds, Inc. ("Meeder")  to
provide discretionary investment management services for the City's operating portfolio, pursuant  to
California Governtnent Code §53607 and the City's adopted Investment Policy.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council  will  consider:
  a.  Approve a Professional Services Agreement with Meeder Public Funds, Inc. for discretionary
  investment management services for an initial term of three (3) years, with up to two (2) one-year
  renewal options at the City's sole discretion, for a total term not to exceed five (5) years; and
  b.  Authorize the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form approved as to form by the City Attorney.

FISCAL IMPACT:  Compensation under this Agreement is asset-based, tiered, and all-inclusive.  Fees are
calculated monthly in arrears on the market value of assets under management (AUM):

staff, annual City Council presentation, and staff training and education. No additional costs may be
incurred without prior written authorization from the Director of Administrative  Services.

investment portfolio currently totals approximately $100 million, subject to market fluctuation and seasonal
cash flow variation.

 At the current  portfolio  size, the management  fee represents  approximately  6.5 -7  basis points  of assets
under  management.  While  investment  returns  are subject  to market  conditions  and cannot  be guaranteed,
professional  active  management  may  improve  portfolio  structuring,  credit  surveillance,  and  maturity

liquidity,  and yield.

EXECUTIVE  SUMMARY:  Following  a formal  competitive  procurement  process  (RFP No.  FIN-2025-
01),  staff  recommend  awarding  a Professional  Services  Agreement  to  Meeder  Public  Funds,  Inc,
("Meeder")  for discretionary  investment  management  of the City's  core operating  portfolio.  Meeder  was
determined  to be the most  qualified  firm,  offering  strong  public-sector  experience,  a robust  compliance
framework,  competitive  fees, and institutional-grade  reporting  capabilities.

The  Agreement  provides  comprehensive  portfolio  management  services  -  including  active  maturity
laddering,  continuous  credit  monitoring,  and quarterly  performance  reviews  -  at an estimated  all-inclusive
annual  cost of $65,000-$70,000  based on the current  portfolio  size of approximately  $100 million.  All  fees
include  meetings,  reporting,  training,  and related  expenses.  No additional  compensation  is payable  without
prior  written  approval.

The Agreement  is structured  in compliance  with  California  Government  Code §§53600  et seq., §53607,  the
City's  adopted  Investment  Policy,  and all applicable  procurement  requirements.

BACKGROUND:  The City  issued  Request  for Proposals  No.  FIN-2025-01  for Investment  Management
Services  in accordance  with  the City's  purchasing  policies  and competitive  procurement  requirements.  The
RFP sought  a qualified,  SEC-registered  investment  adviser  to provide  discretionary  portfolio  management
for the City's  operating  funds,  consistent  with  California  Government  Code  §§ 53600  et seq., the annual
delegation  of authority  under  § 53607,  and the City's  adopted  Investment  Policy.

Proposals  were evaluated  by a review  committee  based on criteria  including:
  *  Public-sector  experience,  qualifications,  and client  references
  *  Investment  philosophy,  risk management  framework,  and compliance  program
  @  Reporting  capabilities,  technology  platform,  and service  delivery
  *  Cybersecurity  protocols  and data protection  standards
  *  Fee structure  and overall  cost competitiveness

Following  evaluation  of written  proposals  and any applicable  interviews,  Meeder  Public  Funds,  Inc. was
determined  to be the most qualified  firm  and to provide  the best overall  value to the City.

ANALYSIS:  The City  maintains  a fiduciary  responsibility  to safeguard  public  funds  in accordance  with
State law and Council-adopted  policy.  Engaging  a qualified  SEC-registered  investment  adviser  strengthens
institutional  controls  while  preserving  Council's  annual  delegation  authority  under  Government  Code
§53607.

Under  California  Government  Code  §53607,  the City  Council  may  delegate  investment  authority  to the
Director  of Administrative  Services  on an annual  basis.  The  Agreement  is structured  to support  this
delegation  framework:  Meeder  provides  professional  portfolio  management  under  the  direction  and
oversight  of the Director,  consistent  with  the City's  Investment  Policy.  The statutory  investment  priority
hierarchy  -  safety  of principal,  liquidity,  and yield,  in that order -  remains  the governing  framework  for
all portfolio  decisions.

 Under  the Agreement,  Meeder  will  provide  the following  services  on an ongoing  basis:
  *  Maturity  laddering  aligned  with  City  cash flow  forecasts,  continuous  credit  monitoring,  and active

  *  Strict  adherence  to the City's  Investment  Policy,  with  investments  executed  only through  qualified
  broker-dealers  consistent  with  Policy  requirements
  *  Monthly  portfolio  statements,  quarterly  performance  review  meetings  with  Finance  staff,  and at
  least one annual  presentation  to the City  Council
  *  Conflict-of-interest  protections  consistent  with  the Agreement's  affiliated-product  restrictions  and
  disclosure  requirements
  *  Ongoing  training  and market  education  for staff, provided  at no additional  cost

The Agreement  includes  explicit  safeguards  addressing  potential  conflicts  arising  from  Meeder's  or its
affiliates'  interests  in  Local  Government  Investment  Pools  (LGIPs),  money  market  funds,  and  other
financial  products.  Meederhas  disclosed  these relationships  in Exhibit  C (Terms  of Services-Discretionary
Accounts).  Notwithstanding  those disclosures,  the Agreement  prohibits  investment  in any affiliated  product
without  prior  written  approval  from  the  Director  and requires  full  fee disclosure  upon  request.  This
provision  takes precedence  over Exhibit  C.

The Agreement  also incorporates  California  Levine  Act  (Gov.  Code  §84308)  disclosure  requirements,
which  Meeder  is required  to satis:ty prior  to Council  approval.

This  structure  improves  internal  control  and oversight  while  allowing  Finance  staff to focus  on treasury
management,  forecasting,  and broader  fiscal  strategy.  The proposed  Agreement  reflects  industry-standard
protections,  clear order-of-precedence  terms,  defined  insurance  requirements,  cybersecurity  safeguards,  and
enforceable  proposal  cornrnitments.  Staff  recommend  approval  as it represents  a prudent  enhancement  to
the City's  investment  governance  framework.

7. SCOPE  OF  SERVICES  / REQUIREMENT  SPECIFICATIONS
The Investment  Manager  shall provide  full-service  discretionary  investment  management
for the City's core operating  funds  in accordance  with the City's Investment  Policy and
applicable  law. Services  shall include,  but are not limited to:

  A.  Develop  and implement  an investment  strategy  consistent  with the City's
  Investment  Policy, cash-flow  requirements,  and risk parameters.
  B.  Buy and sell authorized  securities  on a delivery-versus-payment  (DVP) basis and
  maintain  documentation  demonstrating  best execution  for all trades.
  C. Coordinate  maturities  with the City's projected  cash-flow  needs and collaborate
  annually  with staff to review  and refine cash-flow  forecasts.  The Accounting  and
  Finance  Manager  will provide  liquidity  forecasts  on a regular  basis.
  D. Conduct  credit and counterparty  due diligence,  including  broker/dealer  approval
  reviews  and ongoing  monitoring  of issuers,  custodial  institutions,  and depository
  banks.
  E.  Provide  ongoing  market  and economic  research,  interest-rate  outlooks,  and
  scenario  analyses  to support  strategic  decisions.
  F.  Prepare  quarterly  performance  and compliance  reports  meeting  California  Gov.
  Code § 53646 and provide  monthly  transaction  and holding  summaries.  Each
  quarterly  report shall include  portfolio  composition,  sector  distribution,  yield,
  duration,  and performance  versus  the approved  benchmark,  and shall
  incorporate  balances  in LAIF or other authorized  investment  pools.

Terms of Services  Discretionary  Accounts
Meeder  Pubfic Funds

  The following Terms of Services are applicable to services offered by Meeder Public Funds, Inc. ("Meeder")  and
shall be incorporated into any agreement for investment advisory services ("Agreement").

  L  Investment  Management  Services.  Client appoints  Meeder as discretionary investment  manager to
invest, reinvest and mariage tt'ie secvrities, cash and other  assets of the Account subject to the investment
guidelines ('investment  Guidelines") provided by Client.

  2, Trading Authorization.  Client grants Meeder discretionary trading authority and appoints Meeder as agent
and attorney-in-fact  with respect to investments in the Account. Meeder may direct the purchase, sale, exchange,
conversion,  delivery or other acquisition or disposition of securities and other investments in the Account and act on
behalf of Client in all other matters incidental to the handling of Account investments, all without prior consultation
with Client.

  3. Custody. Meeder will not assume physical custody of the Account or any portion of it. Client shall establish
a custodial account with a qualified custodian ("Custodian").  Client will receive from the Custodian  account
statements  and confirmations  identifying assets and transactions  in the Account.  All transactions  will be
consummated  by payment to, or delivery by, the Custodian of all cash, securities and other assets due to or from
the Account. The Custodian shall be responsible For investing any daily cash balances in the Account and Meeder
will not exercise discretion to select sweep vehicles For the Account.

  4, Investment  Objectives  and Restrictions.  Client may provide Meeder with an Investment  Policy
Statement or other written directions setting forth the investment objectives and any specific investment restrictions
or limitations which govern the Account. Meeder shall be entitled to rely on such guidelines,  objectives and
restrictions relating to the Account as it may receive from Client. It is Client's responsibility to inform Meeder in
writing of any changes or modifications to these directions, which shall be given ten days in advance of any such
change.

  5. Fees. For the services provided in accordance with this Agreement, Client shall pay Meeder an annual fee
("Fee") on terms set forth in the Agreement to which these Terms of Service apply. Where Client has elected to
have fees deducted from the Account, Client authorizes the Custodian to deduct fees from the Account and pay
them to Meeder. The account statements will reflect the fee amount withdrawn in any period. Client is responsible
for notifying Meeder of any exceptions or objections to the amount billed within thirty days from the billing date.

  6. Brokerage.  Unless otherwise directed, Meeder will place trades for the Account through such brokers or
dealers as it may select. When selecting brokers, Meeder's primary consideration  will be the broker's ability to
provide best execution of trades and Meeder may consider the quality and reliability of the brokerage services,
trade price and commission, as well as research and other services provided by the broker-deaiers.

  7. Trade Aggregation.  Meeder may aggregate trades for multiple clients when, in the adviser's judgment,
aggregation is in the best interests of the clients involved. Orders are aggregated to facilitate best execution and
each client participating in the aggregated transaction receives the same price and participation in such trade on a
pro-rata basis. Where it is not possible to obtain the same execution price for all securities purchased or sold on an
aggregated  basis, Meeder will follow its trade allocation  policy, which is designed to ensure that securities
atlocations are made in a fair and equitable manner.

  8. Promoter Arrangements.  Meeder accepts Clients referred through unaffiliated third parties ("Promoters")
and may pay cash compensation  for the endorsement of Meeder's services, which provides the Promoter with an
incemive to refer clients. Clients  will not incur additional fees for being reTeaed to Meeder by a Promoter. Clients

 that engage Meeder as their investment adviser following a referral by a Promoter will receive a written disclosure
statementdescribing the nature and terms of the arrangement,includingthe amount payableto the Promoter.

  9. Local Government Investment Pools. Where appropriate, Meeder may recommend the use of a Local
Government Investment Pool ("LGIP") in which Meeder or one of its affiliates earn advisory and/or administration
fees. Assets p!aced in an LGIP are not included among eligible assets when calculating the investment advisory
fee. Because Meeder or its affiliates receive fees in connectionwith programs we sponsor or recommend, use of
these programs presents a conflict of interest. By investing in an LGIP, Client specifically consents to the conflicts
presented by such investment and payment of fees.

  10. Custodial Sweep Vehicles. Where available, Meeder may recommend the use of the Meeder
GovernmentMoney Market Fund as a vehicle to sweep cash held in the custodial accountfor investment. Because
Meeder's affiliates earn advisory, transfer agency and administration fees for management of the Meeder
Government Money Market Fund, recommendationof the fund as a sweep vehicle presents a conflict of interest.
Meeder charges investment advisory fees on the total market value of assets held in the custodial account,
including sweep vehicles. By selecting the Meeder GovernmentMoney Market Fund, Client specifically consents to
the conflicts presented by such investment and payment of fees.

  11. Third-Party Payments. Meeder or its affiliates receive compensation from unaffiliated third parties for
endorsingor recommendingcertain financial productsto its clients. This arrangement presentsa conflict of interest
because it provides Meeder with an incentive to solicit and secure participation in the program. Asset-based
advisoryfees are not charged for assets invested in productsthat pay indirect compensationto Meeder.

  'l2. Proxy Voting. Meeder does not accept or assume authority to vote proxies for its public fund clients.
Clients will receive their proxies or other solicitations directly from their Custodian. Client agrees that Meeder will
not advise or act for Client in any legal proceedings, including bankruptcies or class actions, involving securities
held or previously held by the Account or the issuers  of such  securities.

  13. Electronic Delivery. Client consents to electronicdelivery of all documents from Meeder, including but not
limited to a copy of the executed Agreement, statements, confirmations, Meeder's Form ADV Part 2 and
amendments thereto, and other general communicationsdelivered to Client's electronic mail address of record.
Delivery of communicationsto Clients in this Tashionwill be deemed effective unless Meeder is notified otherwise.
Client is responsiblefor maintainingan accurate and up to date email address and to ensure that Client at a!l times
has the ability to receive communications  directed in this manner.

  14. Confidentiality. All information and advice furnished by either party to the other, including their respective
agents and employees, shall be treated as confidential and shall not be disclosed to third parties except as
otherwise required by law or as agreed to in writing by Client. Notwithstandingthe foregoing, Client consents to the
use of Client's name in sales and marketing material used by Meeder or its affiliates solely for the purpose of
identifying the Client as an investment advisory client.

  15. Services to Other Clients. Client understandsthat Meeder serves as investment adviser for other Clients
and will continue to do so. Client also understands that Meeder, its personnel and affiliates ("Affiliated Persons")
may give advice or take action in performing their duties to other clients, or for their own accounts, that differ from
advice given to or action taken for Client. Meeder is not obligated to buy, sell or recommend For Client any security
or other investment that Meeder or its Affiliated Persons may buy, sell or recommend for any other client or their
own accounts.

  16. Meeder's Representahons. Meeder represents that it is a registered investment adviser  under  the
Investment  Advisers  Act or I 940.

  17. Client's Representahons. Client represents and acknowledges that: (i) Client is the sole owner of the
Account assets and has full power and authority to enter into this Agreement and to commit the assets to Meeder's
management and supervision; (ii) that the person signing this Agreement on behalf of Client is authorized and
empoweredto establish accounts and commit the assets to Meeder's management and supervision on the entity's
behalf; (iii) Client has received Meeder's current Form ADV, Part 2A and B; and (iv) Client has received a copy of
Meeder's  Privacy  Policy.

Privacy  Policy
Meeder  Investment  Management  and the Meeder  Funds are committed  to
maintaining the financial  privacy  of our current,  former  and prospective  customers.
This policy  explains  how we protect  the security  and confidentiality  of our
customer's  information.

PERSONAL  INFORMATION  WE  COLLECT

We may collect information about Meeder customers from a variety of sources, including:

  Information provided by you or your representative on applications or forms, such as your name, address, date of birth, social
  security  number  and investment  objectives;

  Information about the transactions in your account, such as your account balance and transaction history; and

  Information we obtain from third parties regarding you, to verify your identity or transfer your account.

INFORMATION  WE  SHARE  WITH  OUR  AFFILIATES

Our affiliates are financial service providers that offer transfer agency, customer accounting, customer servicing, investment
advisory, and other financial services. We share information with our affiliates to service your account. In addition, we may also
share information with our affiliates to alert you to other products or services offered by Meeder to the extent provided by law.
Information collected from customers whose accounts are opened through investment professionals is not shared with Meeder
affiliates  for marketing  purposes.

INFORMATION  WE  SHARE  WITH  THIRD  PARTIES

On occasion, we share information we collect about you with unaffiliated third parties to perform services in connection with your
account, such as processing transactions, preparing and mailing account statements, and other forms of customer servicing.
Information provided to third parties may not be used for any other purpose and Meeder does not permit unaffiliated third parties
to use customer  information to market their products or services.

HOW  WE  PROTECT  INFORMATION  ABOUT  YOU

We maintain policies, and require all unaffiliated third parties to maintain policies, to safeguard customerinformation. We restrict
access to nonpublic personal information about you to those persons who need to know thatinformation in orderto provide products
and services to you. We also maintain physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards to guard your nonpublic personal information.

WHO  THIS  POLICY  APPLIES  TO

This policy applies to customers who open relationships directly with Meeder. It applies to Meeder Funds and Meeder's affiliated
companies, including Meeder Asset Management, Meeder Advisory Services, Meeder Public Funds, Meeder Distribution Services
and Mutual Funds Service Company.

QUESTIONS

Contact us at 800-325-3539  or visit us online at www.meederinvestment.com

ANALYSIS:

Public  Works  - Electric  Trucks
The Public Works Department operates 90 vehicles essential to maintaining the City's streets, sewers,
and water infrastructure. Six aging trucks, that are used by the Street and Sewer Division and Water
Division, have exceeded their recommended service life and are proposed for replacement. These
vehicles exhibit high maintenance costs, frequent breakdowns, and elevated emissions.

Staff recommend replacing them with 2026 Chevrolet Silverado electric trucks. On August 26, 2025,
the City Council authorized the purchase of Ford F-150 Lightning electric trucks for this purpose;
however, Ford subsequently discontinued that model. The Chevrolet Silverado is the recommended
substihite.

Electric trucks reduce fuel costs, lower emissions, and support compliance with California Air
Resources Board (CARB)  requirements. New vehicles will be outfitted with safety lighting,
toolboxes, and required equipment before being placed into service, with delivery expected
approximately 16 weeks after Council  approval.

Police Department  -  Detective  Vehicles

The Police Detective Bureau relies on dependable vehicles for investigations,  surveillance,
interagency coordination, and task force assignments. Two vehicles are proposed for replacement:

Both  vehicles  have exceeded  their  optimal  service  life and are experiencing  increasing  maintenance
demands.  The  Police  Chief  has reviewed  and accepted  the NCL  Tax  Exempt  Municipal  Lease
Proposal  dated  January  28, 2026;  however,  upon  further  financial  analysis,  direct  acquisition  is
recommended  as the more  cost-effective  approach.  The not-to-exceed  authorization  allows  staff  to
procure  substantially  equivalent  vehicles  if specific  inventory  is unavailable  prior  to purchase  order
issuance.

Procurement  Approach
Both  vehicle  purchases  will  be made through  the Sourcewell  Cooperative  Purchasing  Program  under
Contract  No.  091521-NAF  with  National  Auto  Fleet  Group  (72 Hour  LLC  dba National  Auto  Fleet
Group).  Sourcewell  is a State of Minnesota  local  government  unit that administers  competitively  bid
cooperative  contracts  available  to public  agencies  nationwide.  Use of this contract  satisfies  the City's
competitive  purchasing  requirements  under the South Gate Municipal  Code, eliminating  the need for
a separate  formal  bid process  while  ensuring  fair and transparent  pricing.

BACKGROUND:  The City maintains  a Fleet Master  Plan to guide vehicle  replacement  decisions
across all departments.  The Plan establishes  recommended  service  life cycles  based on mileage,  age,
maintenance  cost trends,  and operational  demands.  All  vehicles  proposed  for replacement  in this
report  were  identified  in the Plan  as overdue  for  retirement,  in some  cases since  2019  or 2021.
Proactive  fleet  management  reduces  overall  lifecycle  costs and minimizes  operational  disruptions
caused by unexpected  mechanical  failures.

Vehicle  market  conditions  remain  dynamic,  with  dealership  inventory  levels  changing  rapidly.  The
not-to-exceed  authorization  structure  adopted  for the detective  vehicle  purchase,  and the flexibility
to substitute  a comparable  electric  truck  for the Silverado  should  it become  unavailable,  reflect  this
reality  and protect  the City's  ability  to complete  timely  acquisitions  within  approved  :tunding  limits.

  SUBJECT:  RECEIVE  AND  FILE  THE  FISCAL  YEAR  2024-25  ANNUAL
  COMPREHENSIVE  FINANCIAL  REPORT

  PURPOSE:  To present  the City  of South  Gate's  Fiscal  Year  2024-25  Annual  Comprehensive
  Financial  Report  (ACFR)  to the City  Council  for review.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  Recommendation  to receive  and file  the City  of South  Gate's
  Aru'iual  Comprehensive  Financial  Report  (ACFR)  for the Fiscal  Year Ended  June 30, 2025.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  associated  with  the recornrnended  action.  The item
  is informational  and fulfills  the City's  annual  financial  reporting  requirement  under  California
  Government  Code.

  ANALYSIS:  The presentation  of the City's  Annual  Comprehensive  Financial  Report  (ACFR)  is
  an important  element  of the City's  cornrnitment  to financial  transparency,  accountability,  and
  responsible  fiscal  stewardship

  The ACFR  reports  the City's  financial  results  for the fiscal  year that ended  June 30, 2025.  While
  it provides  a comprehensive  record  of the City's  financial  activity  during  that period,  it does not
  reflect  fiscal  pressures  that  have  developed  since  that  date  and are currently  being  evaluated
  through  the City's  ongoing  budget  development  process.  The Annual  Comprehensive  Financial
  Report  (ACFR)  presents  the City's  audited  financial  statements  for the fiscal  year ended June 30,
  2025.  The report  was prepared  by the Administrative  Services  Department  in accordance  with
  Generally  Accepted  Accoiu'iting  Principles  (GAAP)  established  by the Governrnental  Accounting
  Standards  Board  (GASB).

  California  Governrnent  Code and City  Ordinance  require  that the City  prepare  an annual  financial
  report  and have it audited  by an independent  certified  public  accounting  firm.

  The City's  independent  auditors,  Davis  Farr LLP,  conducted  the audit  of the financial  statements
  for the fiscal  year  ended  June 30, 2025.  The  auditors  issued  an unmodified  ("clean")  opinion,
  indicating  that the financial  statements  fairly  present  the City's  financial  position  and results  of

  329
 operations  in accordance  with  Generally  Accepted  Accounting  Principles.  The completion  of the
aru'iual  audit  represents  a key  component  of the City's  financial  accountability  framework  and
provides  independent  assurance  regarding  the accuracy  of the City's  financial  reporting.

It is important  to understand  what  the audit  opinion  represents.  A clean audit  confirnns  that the
City's  financial  statements  are fairly  presented  in accordance  with  accounting  standards.  It does
not indicate  that the City's  operating  budget  is structurally  balanced  or that the City  is not facing
fiscal  challenges.

The ACFR  presents  the City's  financial  position  on a government-wide  basis  and includes  all
funds,  capital  assets, restricted  resources,  and long-term  obligations  under  accrual  accounting.
Because  these  statements  include  the long-term  value  of infrastructure  and legally  restricted
resources,  they often  present  a stronger  financial  position  than what  is available  to fund  day-to-
day municipal  services.

ACFR  Financial  Highlights

As reported  in the ACFR,  the City's  governrnent-wide  net position  totaled  approximately  $324.1
million  as of June 30, 2025,  representing  an increase  of $16.2 million  from  the prior  fiscal  year.
This  increase  primarily  reflects  capital  asset  activity,  restricted  funds,  and  other  long-term
accounting  factors  rather  than changes  in discretionary  General  Fund operating  capacity.

The  City  reported  approximately  $352  million  in capital  assets, net of depreciation,  reflecting
continued  investment  in  infrastructure  such  as streets,  water  and  sewer  systems,  and  public
facilities.

During  Fiscal  Year  2024-25,  the City  implemented  Governmental  Accounting  Standards  Board
(GASB)  Statement  No. 101, Compensated  Absences,  which  refined  the accounting  treatment  for
employee  leave liabilities.  Implementation  resulted  in a prior-period  adjustment  to beginning  net
position  but did not impact  cash balances  or the City's  operating  results.

Understanding  the ACFR  in the Context  of South  Gate's  Fiscal  Reality

This report  reflects  the City's  financial  position  as of June 30, 2025,  prior  to the fiscal  pressures
currently  being  addressed  through  the FY 2026-27  budget  process.  The City's  government-wide
net position  of $324.1 million  may  suggest  financial  strength  to the average  reader. It is critical
that this figure  be understood  for what  it actually  represents  -  and what it does not.

A substantial  portion  of that $324. I million  consists  of capital  assets: streets,  water  mains,  sewer
lines,  parks,  and public  buildings  -  infrastructure  that cannot  be liquidated  or redirected  to pay
for police  officers,  recreation  programs,  or any other  municipal  service.  A significant  portion  of
the remaining  balance  is held  in restricted  funds  legally  required  for specific  purposes,  such as
federal  grants,  water  and sewer  operations,  and capital  improvement  programs.  These  dollars  are
not available  to fund general  City  services.

  330
 The General  Fund  finances  most  day-to-day  municipal  services  residents  experience,  including
police  patrols,  code enforcement,  park maintenance,  street cleaning,  and City Hall  operations.  The
General  Fund is currently  facing  significant  structural  fiscal  pressure.

The Structural  Fiscal  Pressures  of the General  Fund

For several  years, the City's  General  Fund has spent more than it collects on recurring  revenues.
The gap was masked  in recentyears  by one-time federal American Rescue  Plan Act  (ARPA)  funds,
which  were used to sustain  service  levels  while  longer-term  solutions  were evaluated.  Those 'funds
are no longer  available  and will  not recur.
What  remains  is a structural  imbalance  -  meaning  the City's  ongoing  operating  costs exceed  its

ongoing  revenues,  and there is no reserve  left to bridge  the gap. The primary  cost drivers  are not
discretionary:  they include  mandatory  pension  contributions  to CalPERS,  workers'  compensation
and liability  insurance  premiums,  and employee  health  benefits  -  all of which  automatically
increase  each year regardless  of budget  decisions  made at the local  level.

The City  is currently  projecting  a General  Fund structural  deficit  of approximately  $9.4 million  in
Fiscal  Year  2026-27.  To place  that in context:  the City's  entire  General  Fund  revenue  base is

approximately  $71 million,  with  adopted  expenditures  at approximately  $78.2 million.  A $9.4
million  shortfall  represents  roughly  13 percent  of all General  Fund revenues;  a deficit  of significant
magnitude  for a city of South  Gate's  size and budget  structure.

What  Closing  This  Deficit  Actually  Means

A balanced  budget  is legally  required,  and the  City  will  produce  one. But  the public  should

understand  what balancing  the budget  without  new recurring  revenue  will  require.

Cutting  $9.4 million  from  a $78.2 million  operating  budget  means eliminating  more than one dollar
out of every  eight the City  spends delivering  services.

Because  the General  Fund  finances  the City's  core municipal  operations,  addressing  a deficit  of

this  magnitude  would  likely  require  adjustments  to  staffing  levels,  service  delivery,  facility
operations,  and community  programs.  Based  on the City's  current  budget  projections,  addressing
a deficit  of  this  magnitude  through  expenditure  reductions  alone  could  require  adjustments
including:

  @  Reductions  in Police  Department  staffing  and services  -  including  fewer  officers  available
  for  patrol,  longer  response  times  to  non-emergency  calls,  and  reduced  capacity  for

  community  policing  and investigations;
  *  Closure  or significantly  reduced  operating  hours  at City  recreation  centers,  parks,  and
  community  facilities;
  *  Reduced  public  works  maintenance,  including  street  repair,  graffiti  abatement,  and

  landscape  maintenance  in City  parks and rights-of-way;
  @  Elimination  or significant  reduction  of community  programs,  senior  services,  and youth
  progratnming;
  *  Substantial  reductions  in City  staffing  across  multiple  departments,  affecting  residents'
  day-to-day  ability  to access City  services.

  331
 These  examples  illustrate  the types of service impacts  that could  occur  if the structural  deficit  is
addressed  solely  through  expenditure  reductions.

The Path  Fonvard
The ACFR  presented  tonight  accurately  reports  the City's  financial  activity  through  June 30, 2025
and confirms  that the City met all financial  obligations  during  that  period.  It is appropriately
presented as a receive-and-file item.

However,  the ACFR  does not, and by design  caru'iot, capture  the fiscal  pressures  the City's  General
Fund now  faces. The ACFR  is a backward-looking  accounting  document  prepared  under  accrual-
based  governrnental  accounting  standards.  The  fiscal  pressures  the  City  currently  faces  is a
forward-looking  policy  reality  that will  be resolved  through  the FY 2026-27  budget  process.

The City  Council  may consider  policy  options  to address the structural  deficit,  including  potential
revenue  measures,  expenditure  reductions,  or a combination  of both.  The  service  and staffing
adjustments  described  above  represent  the likely  outcome  absent new recurring  revenue  or other
policy  action.

Residents  and stakeholders  who review  this ACFR  should  do so with  full awareness  that the City's
audited  financial  position  as of June 30, 2025  does not  re:flect  the difficult  and consequential
decisions  that lie ahead in Fiscal  Year 2026-27  and beyond.

BACKGROUND:  The Annual  Comprehensive  Financial  Report  (ACFR)  is the City's  official
audited  financial  report  prepared  in accordance  with  accounting  standards  established  by the
Governrnental  Accounting  Standards  Board  (GASB).  The  report  includes  the City's  financial
statements,  notes, and statistical  information  regarding  the City's  financial  condition.

The ACFR  differs  from  the aru'iual budget.  While  the budget  is a forward-looking  policy  document
that establishes  spending  authority  and service  priorities,  the ACFR  reports  the actual  financial
results  of the prior  fiscal  year.

Key  highlights  of  the  City's  financial  performance  are  summarized  in  the  Management's
Discussion  and Analysis  (MD&A)  section  of the ACFR,  which  provides  an overview  of financial
results,  changes  in fund balances,  and economic  factors  affecting  the City.

The City's  Federal  Single  Audit,  which  evaluates  compliance  with  federal  grant requirements,  will
be presented  to the City  Council  separately  once finalized.

SOUTH  GATE  PROFILE

The City of South Gate, incorporated  on January 20, 1923, under the general laws of the State of
California.  South  Gate encompasses  7.4 square miles  and is in the heart of the Los Angeles
Metropolitan  area. The city is characterized  by a high-density,  working-class  community  with  a
population  of 92,955  according  to the State of California  Department  of Finance.  Services
provided  by the City include  administration,  police, public  works,  planning,  building  & safety, and
parks & recreation.  The City  of South Gate provides  a fiill  range of services  for the citizens
delivered  by the City's  own employees.  The City has its own Police Department  but contracts  for
fire services through  the Los Angeles  County  Fire Department  (LACFD),  and contracts  with other
governmental  entities  or private  companies  for library  and refuse collection.

Centrally  located,  South  Gate is an ideal  location  for  commerce  within  a 15-mile  radius  of
downtown  Los Angeles,  Los Angeles  International  Airport,  and the Ports of Los Angeles  and Long
Beach.  The city is linked  to these sites by several major  transportation  thoroughfares,  including
the I-710 (Long  Beach) and I-105 (Century)  freeways,  Firestone  and Alameda  Boulevards,  and an
extensive  rail system with  services provided  by the Union  Pacific  and Southem  Pacific  Railroads,
With  a diverse mix of residential,  commercial,  and industrial  areas, the City has promoted  itself as
an area  rich in economic  opportunities  and continues  to have many projects  slated for development
that will  play a significant  role in revitalizing  the community.

The City has operated under the council-manager  form of government  since incorporation.  Policy-
making  and legislative  authority  are vested in the goveming  City Council,  which  consists  of five
Council  Members,  including  the Mayor  and Vice-Mayor.  The City Council  is responsible  for,
among  other things,  passing  ordinances,  adopting  the budget,  appointing  committees,  and hiring
the City Manager  and the City Attorney.  The City Council  is elected on a non-partisan,  at-large
basis.  Council  Members  are elected  to four-year  staggered  temis  with  two  or three  Council
Members  elected every two years.  Each year, the City Council  selects the Mayor  and Vice Mayor
for a one-year  term.

Overview  of the Financial  Statements

This Management's  Discussion  and Analysis  (MD&A)  presents  management's  narrative  interpretation  of the City of
South  Gate's  financial  performance  and  condition  for  the  fiscal  year  ended  June  30,  2025.  It is intended  to
complement,  not duplicate,  the  accompanying  basic financial  statements  and should  be read  in conjunction  with
those  statements  and the related  notes.

The City's financial  statements  are presented  from  two complementary  perspectives.  The government-wide  financial
statements  provide  a long-term,  economic  view  of the City as a whole  using the accrual  basis of accounting.  T hese
statements  report  all assets, deferred  outflows  of resources,  liabilities,  and deferred  inflows,  including  capital  ASSETS

and long-term  obligations  such as pensions,  other  postemployment  benefits  (OPEB), leases, and bonded  debt.

The fund  financial  statements  focus  on the  City's  near-term  financial  position  and results  of operations  using the
modified  accrual  basis of accounting.  These  statements  emphasize  fiscal  accountability  by reporting  balances  of
spendable  resources  and demonstrating  compliance  with  the legally  adopted  budget.

Together,  these  perspectives  illustrate  both  the  City's  annual  operating  results  and  its  longer-term  fiscal
commitments.

Fiscal Snapshot:  Fiscal Year 2024-25

While  the City"s government-wide  net position  increased  by 516.2 million  during FY 2024-25  and total fund balances
remained  positive,  these  headline  figures  do not fully  reflect  the City's  long-term  operating  dynamics.  The increase
in government-wide  net position  primarily  reflects  accounting  recognition  of capital  assets, restricted  resources,  and
other  non-operating  factors,  rather  than changes  in discretionary  General  Fund operating  capacity.

The General  Fund, which  suppods  core municipal  services  such as public  safety,  parks, and general  government,  has
experienced  a recurring  pattern  in which  ongoing  expenditures  have  exceeded  ongoing  revenues  in recent  fiscal
years,  resulting  in the planned  use of one-time  resources  and fund  balance  as part of adopted  budgets.  In recent
fiscal years, this gap was addressed  through  the use of one-time  resources,  most notably  approximately  S18 million
in federal  American  Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding,  along with  interfund  transfers  and planned  use of fund  balance.

As ARPA resources  have been  largely  expended,  future  budgets  will  increasingly  require  policy  decisions  regarding
service  levels,  expenditure  controls,  and the  identification  of sustainable  recurring  revenues.  These  conditions
represent  a long-term  operating  and policy consideration  rather  than a liquidity  or solvency  issue. Management  does
not believe  the City will have difficulty  meeting  its financial  obligations  as they come due.

The discussion  that  follows  presents  the City's  financial  results  in accordance  with  generally  accepted  accounting
principles,  beginning  with  the  government-wide  perspective  and then  focusing  on individual  funds,  including  the
General  Fund.

requirements and near-term fiscal flexibility.

As of June 30, 2025, the City's Bovernmental funds reported ending fund balances of !>67.6M, a decrease of S4.2M
(5.9%) from the prior year. Of that amount, 92.OM is a nonspendable fund balance. Of the remaining S65.6M
spendable fund balance, S43.6M is restricted because it is subject to external enforceable legal obligations, S20.7M
iS committed far SuChTHINGS  aS an emergency reSerVej  a budget StabiliZatiOn fund, and an OPEB SeCtiOn 115 trust,
